# ORIGINAL ABSTRACT: Policymakers are increasingly concerned about the revival of superpower conflict. Increased competition among great powers has been especially evident in the exercise of foreign influence, where Russia and China have increased their efforts to influence less powerful nations. To date, the absence of quantitative data has limited systematic investigation of this resurgence of authoritarian influence activity. We introduce a new, country-month dataset tracking reports of influence by Russia and China in 66 aid-receiving low- and middle-income countries from 2012 through August 2025. We construct the data by applying large language models (LLMs) to an original corpus of more than 120 million news articles sourced from high-quality, domestic news sources and use it to describe trends in influence activity over time and across countries. Finally, as a test case, use the data to examine Russian influence activity in the months before the invasion of Ukraine. We document a dramatic, previously undetected, pre-invasion surge in diplomacy and hard power reporting across many countries. In doing so, we show that this data is useful for both theory testing and foreign policy decision-making.

## Data availability

The primary public-facing resource for the Resurgent Authoritarian Influence (RAI) project is our interactive website and dashboard: https://web.sas.upenn.edu/mlp-devlab/rai/rai-overview/. It allows researchers to explore reported influence activity over time by target country, influencing country (China or Russia), thematic category, and individual indicator. The country–month RAI data and replication materials for all analyses reported in this article are available in the article’s GitHub replication repository: https://github.com/ML4PDevLab/RAI-Paper. The broader MLP data-construction pipeline and regularly updated RAI data are maintained separately in the ML4P data repository: https://github.com/ML4PDevLab/MLP-data-intro. Researchers seeking alternative temporal aggregations, including weekly data, may submit a request through the ML4P data request form.

## Declaration of AI usage (if applicable)
We employed artificial intelligence tools specific states of the data production and validation pipeline. As described in the manuscript and appendix, we fine-tuned a ModernBERT-large transformer model to classify news articles into 21 influence categories, and trained a neural network model to detect surges in influence reporting. To accommodate non-English sources, we used neural machine translation models via Hugging Face and OpenNMT to translate articles into English prior to classification. Finally, we used GPT-4 to assist with qualitative validation: for each country-month change-point identified in the pre-invasion window, we prompted GPT-4 to summarize the key developments reported in the relevant HQMARC articles, and then assessed whether those summaries indicated genuine Russian influence activity or misclassification. 

We also used Claude Sonnet 4.6 to assist in copyediting. We did not use any AI tools to generate text for any part of the manuscript and appendix.
